ai.summary: This systematic review looked at 17 studies of supportive care models for parents with premature infants in NICUs. It identified six models, including family-centred care, kangaroo mother care, peer support and specialised father support, and found they are linked to reduced parental stress, greater parental engagement and efficacy, and better health outcomes for parents.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that structured support for parents during a baby’s NICU stay can matter for family wellbeing, which is useful for anyone wanting to understand how hospitals might help families cope.
ai.life_skill: Notice what support services are available for parents in a neonatal unit and consider using them if you or someone you know is affected.
ai.fact: Six supportive care models for parents of premature infants in NICUs were identified in the review.

quiz.question: How many supportive care models for parents of premature infants in NICUs did the review identify?
quiz.answer: The review identified six possible supportive care models.

ai.caveat: It is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, and most of the included studies were rated only moderate quality.

items.title: Effectiveness of Stepped Care Psychological Interventions in Children and Adolescents: A Meta-Analytic Review

ai.headline: Stepped care mental health support for young people works about as well as usual care but costs less.
ai.summary: This preprint reviewed studies of stepped care, where children and adolescents start with lighter support and move to more intensive help only if needed. It found similar mental health outcomes to standard care, including intensive treatments, but significantly lower costs.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how mental health services might help more young people without spending more money.
ai.life_skill: Notice if your mental health support feels too intense or too light, and ask a trusted adult or professional about other options.
ai.fact: About 46% of young people in the reviewed studies moved from the first step of care to a later step.

quiz.question: Did stepped care produce better mental health results than control conditions?
quiz.answer: No, effects compared with control conditions were small and non-significant, meaning outcomes were comparable rather than superior.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, so its findings are not final proof.

items.title: Effect of nutrition counseling on complementary feeding practices among mothers with children aged 6–23 months in West Gojjam Zone, Northwest Ethiopia: A cluster-randomized controlled trial

ai.headline: Nutrition counseling helped Ethiopian mothers feed young children more appropriately.
ai.summary: A cluster-randomised trial in rural Northwest Ethiopia compared mothers who received monthly Health Belief Model-based nutrition counseling with mothers who received routine education. Counselled mothers were nearly 2.5 times more likely to practice appropriate complementary feeding, and their children were more likely to meet dietary diversity, meal frequency, and acceptable diet targets.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that structured counseling can improve how young children are fed in similar rural communities, supporting child growth and development.
ai.life_skill: Try asking a qualified health worker or nutritionist for practical advice on what and how often to feed a child aged 6–23 months.
ai.fact: Appropriate complementary feeding is essential for children’s growth and cognitive development.

quiz.question: What did the study find about mothers who received nutrition counseling compared with those who received routine education?
quiz.answer: They were nearly 2.5 times more likely to practice appropriate complementary feeding.

ai.caveat: The results come from one trial in rural Northwest Ethiopia, so they may not apply to other settings.

items.title: Advance Care Planning Impact on the Consistency of Older Adults With Lung Cancer and Their Potential Surrogates Regarding Life-Sustaining Treatment Preferences

ai.headline: A tabletop game helped older adults with lung cancer and their chosen surrogates agree more on life-sustaining treatment choices than a standard manual.
ai.summary: This randomised trial compared an advance care planning tabletop game called “Walking with Wishes” with a standard advance care planning manual in patient–surrogate pairs. The game reduced the gap between patients’ and surrogates’ preferences for five life-sustaining treatments across nine health scenarios, and did not increase state anxiety for either group.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows a simple, low-cost activity can help families understand each other’s wishes about serious medical treatment before a crisis happens.
ai.life_skill: Try talking with a trusted friend or relative about what medical treatments you would or would not want if you became seriously ill.
ai.fact: Advance care planning is the process of discussing and recording preferences for future medical care.
ai.caveat: This is a single trial posted as results on a clinical trials register, so the findings should be treated as preliminary until fully published and peer reviewed.

items.title: The Price of a Chance in Artificial Societies

ai.headline: Reward design changes how simulated agents compete and how much they spend chasing prizes.
ai.summary: Researchers simulated 200 LLM agents competing over 50 rounds to maximise wealth. At low rewards agents invested little, while at high rewards they overcompeted, especially when prize coverage was intermediate. Smaller prizes spread across more winners reduced investment while keeping selection quality similar, but broader coverage lowered selection quality.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how prize structures can shape competition and the costs people bear chasing uncertain rewards.
ai.life_skill: Notice how the size and spread of a prize affects how much effort you are willing to put in.
ai.fact: Agents near the qualification cutoff can invest heavily yet receive no prize and finish poorer than non-winners who invest less.

quiz.question: What happened when smaller prizes were offered to more winners?
quiz.answer: Investment reduced while selection quality was preserved relative to the corresponding top-ability target.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint simulation of artificial LLM agents, not peer-reviewed evidence about real people.

items.title: Sex differences in latent inhibition and their implications for psychotic disorders

ai.headline: Research suggests sex differences in latent inhibition may be linked to psychosis risk, but evidence is mixed.
ai.summary: This systematic review examined studies of latent inhibition in humans and rodents. It found mostly inconclusive evidence for sex differences, though differences were more likely when factors such as drug treatment, juvenile handling, or oestrous phase were involved. New rodent data also suggest sex differences in hippocampal processing during latent inhibition.
ai.why_it_matters: It helps explain how biological sex might influence learning processes linked to hallucinations and delusions in psychosis.
ai.life_skill: Notice how prior exposure to a harmless cue can reduce your attention to it later, and consider whether stress or other factors change that effect for you.
ai.fact: Latent inhibition is the reduced ability to learn about a stimulus after prior exposure to it without consequence.

quiz.question: What did the systematic review find about sex differences in latent inhibition?
quiz.answer: Evidence was predominantly inconclusive and conflicting, with stronger indications of sex differences when additional factors such as drug administration, juvenile handling, or oestrous phase were studied.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, and the underlying evidence is described as mostly inconclusive and conflicting.

items.title: Socio-occupational factors and problematic internet use: indirect associations involving negative affect and impulsivity in a predominantly urban, highly educated Romanian adult sample

ai.headline: Lower social support and work engagement, plus higher work addiction, link to problematic internet use via negative mood and impulsivity.
ai.summary: Researchers surveyed 215 mostly urban, highly educated Romanian adults about internet use, mood, impulsivity, and work factors. Problematic internet use was linked to less perceived social support and work engagement, and more work addiction, anxiety, depression, and impulsivity; negative mood appeared to be a key indirect pathway.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how workplace wellbeing and emotional state may be connected to unhealthy internet habits in adults.
ai.life_skill: Notice whether low mood or work stress makes you use the internet more than you intend.
ai.fact: Problematic internet use was positively associated with work addiction, depressive symptoms, trait anxiety, and impulsivity.

quiz.question: What did the study find about impulsivity alone as a pathway to problematic internet use?
quiz.answer: The indirect association through impulsivity alone was not significant.

ai.caveat: It was a cross-sectional survey, so it cannot show cause and effect or the order in which things happened.

items.title: EPSBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Earnings Forecasting

ai.headline: AI agents can match analyst earnings forecasts but their confidence intervals are often too narrow.
ai.summary: The study tested six AI models on forecasting US company earnings using filings, transcripts and news. Three models were no worse than analyst consensus, while three made larger errors. Across all models, their stated 80% prediction intervals captured actual earnings only 37% to 70% of the time, mostly because forecasts were too low.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that AI tools for financial forecasting may look reasonable on average but can still be overconfident about how uncertain their predictions are.
ai.life_skill: Treat any AI earnings forecast as uncertain and check whether it gives a realistic range rather than a single number.
ai.fact: EPSBench evaluates AI earnings forecasts across 149 firm-quarters from 86 US companies.

quiz.question: How often did the AI models' stated 80% prediction intervals contain the actual reported EPS?
quiz.answer: Only 37% to 70% of the runs that returned an interval, with most misses above the upper bound because forecasts ran low.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint, not yet peer reviewed, and tests only six models on a fixed set of US firm-quarters, so the results may not generalise.

items.title: Type 2 diabetes breakthrough as 54% achieve remission in just 6 months

ai.headline: A low-calorie diet and exercise program helped 54% of younger adults with type 2 diabetes achieve remission in six months.
ai.summary: Researchers studied younger adults with type 2 diabetes who followed an intensive low-calorie diet and structured exercise program. After six months, 54% achieved remission, compared with 4% who received usual care.
ai.why_it_matters: This shows that lifestyle changes may help some younger adults put type 2 diabetes into remission relatively quickly.
ai.life_skill: Talk to a qualified healthcare professional before making major changes to your diet or exercise routine if you have type 2 diabetes.
ai.fact: 54% of participants under age 45 in the intensive program achieved remission compared with 4% receiving usual care.

quiz.question: What percentage of younger adults in the intensive diet and exercise program achieved remission after six months?
quiz.answer: 54% achieved remission, compared with 4% receiving usual care.

ai.caveat: This is a news report, not the full peer-reviewed study, so the findings cannot yet be treated as proven.

items.title: How one of the body's own proteins drives the vicious cycle of inflammation in vaginal yeast infections

ai.headline: A body protein called albumin drives inflammation in vaginal yeast infections while protecting the fungus from immune attack.
ai.summary: The study looked at why immune responses to Candida albicans yeast infections can be intense and persistent. Researchers found that the host protein albumin fuels the inflammatory cascade and at the same time shields the fungal pathogen from the immune system.
ai.why_it_matters: It helps explain why thrush symptoms can be severe and keep coming back, pointing toward new ways to treat recurrent infections.
ai.life_skill: If you keep getting thrush symptoms, see a GP or sexual health clinic rather than repeatedly treating yourself.
ai.fact: Up to three-quarters of women will experience a genital yeast infection at least once in their lives.

quiz.question: What does albumin do in vaginal yeast infections according to the study?
quiz.answer: It fuels the inflammatory cascade while shielding the fungal pathogen from the immune system.

ai.caveat: This is a news report about a single study, not peer-reviewed evidence or proof that changing albumin will treat infections.

items.title: Crop diversification protects fields from extreme weather and boosts productivity

ai.headline: Diversifying crops and keeping soil covered helps farms survive extreme weather and produce more food.
ai.summary: Researchers in Brazil tested how varying crop rotations and maintaining constant soil vegetation affect farm resilience. They found these practices help protect crops from droughts and floods while also increasing overall productivity.
ai.why_it_matters: Understanding how farming methods can adapt to climate extremes helps explain how global food systems might stay stable in a changing world.
ai.life_skill: Notice how variety in your own routines or projects can make you more resilient to unexpected setbacks.
ai.fact: Keeping soil covered with vegetation is linked to better protection against both droughts and floods.

quiz.question: What two weather events does the study say these farming techniques help protect against?
quiz.answer: The techniques help protect crops against droughts and floods.

ai.caveat: This is a news report summarising a specific regional study, so the results may not apply to all climates or farming systems.

items.title: The asteroid killed the dinosaurs. Why did crocodiles survive?

ai.headline: Crocodiles likely survived the dinosaur-extinction asteroid by staying in warm tropical refuges.
ai.summary: Scientists analysed fossils and ancient climate data to investigate why crocodiles survived the mass extinction event 66 million years ago. The findings suggest that their preference for warm environments kept them in tropical areas that remained habitable after the impact.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how specific environmental preferences can help species survive catastrophic global changes, offering insight into how life adapts to extreme shifts.
ai.life_skill: Notice how your own habits or preferences might help you cope with sudden changes in your environment.
ai.fact: Crocodiles are believed to have survived the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction by inhabiting tropical refuges that remained habitable.

quiz.question: Why did crocodiles survive the asteroid impact according to this analysis?
quiz.answer: Their preference for warm environments placed them in tropical refuges that remained habitable.

ai.caveat: This is a news report summarising a scientific analysis, not a peer-reviewed study itself, so the specific mechanisms are presented as a likely explanation rather than proven fact.

items.title: Oxytocin neurons signal state-dependent transitions from rest to thermogenesis and behavioral arousal

ai.headline: Oxytocin-linked brain cells help mice move from rest to warmth and activity.
ai.summary: Scientists studied oxytocin neurons in the hypothalamus of mice. These neurons became active as mice moved from rest to heat production and alertness, in both social and non-social settings. Stimulating the neurons caused warming followed by increased activity.
ai.why_it_matters: It helps explain how the brain may link body temperature control with waking up and becoming active.
ai.life_skill: Try noticing whether you feel slightly warmer just before you become more alert after resting.
ai.fact: Oxytocin neurons in the mouse hypothalamus are linked to transitions from rest to heat production and behavioural arousal.

quiz.question: What happened when researchers stimulated oxytocin neurons in resting mice?
quiz.answer: Heat production increased, followed by behavioural arousal.

ai.caveat: The research was conducted in mice, so it cannot be assumed to apply to humans.

items.title: Strategic Monetary Policy in Open Economies -- by Louphou Coulibaly, Charles Engel

ai.headline: Countries setting their own monetary policy can reach the same outcome as cooperating, but only with full commitment.
ai.summary: The paper studies how two countries should set monetary policy when each government acts only in its own interest. It finds that if policymakers can fully commit in advance, acting alone leads to the same result as cooperating, because financial market prices cancel out any benefit from trying to change trade terms. If commitment is only partial, countries end up worse off.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how a country's interest-rate choices can affect other countries through exchange rates and global financial markets, even when each country only looks after itself.
ai.fact: In this model, changes in financial asset prices remove any advantage a country might gain by using monetary policy to improve its trade terms.

quiz.question: What happens to welfare when countries can only make a partial policy commitment?
quiz.answer: The resulting Nash equilibrium yields lower welfare.

ai.caveat: It is a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, and the findings come from a specific theoretical model rather than real-world evidence.

items.title: A New Map of ‘Empty’ Space Challenges a Tranquil Picture of the Galaxy

ai.headline: Astronomers are using 3D maps to show that the space between stars is dynamic, not static.
ai.summary: Astronomers have long treated the interstellar medium as a static backdrop to the universe. New 3D mapping is revealing that the space between stars is dynamic. This challenges the old picture of a tranquil galaxy.
ai.why_it_matters: It changes our picture of the galaxy by showing that even seemingly empty space is active and changing.
ai.fact: The interstellar medium between stars is dynamic rather than a static backdrop.

quiz.question: What did astronomers traditionally treat the interstellar medium as?
quiz.answer: They treated it as a static backdrop to the goings-on of the universe.

ai.caveat: This is a news summary rather than the original research, so it gives no details about the study’s methods or evidence.

items.title: Rewilding project aims to restore peatland

ai.headline: Cumbria Wildlife Trust has begun repairing damaged peatland at Skiddaw Forest.
ai.summary: Cumbria Wildlife Trust has started work to repair damage to peatland at Skiddaw Forest. The project is described as a rewilding effort to restore the area. The announcement does not yet report any results from the work.

ai.fact: Wildlife trusts carry out rewilding projects to restore damaged peatland.

items.title: Bones may release proteins that slow aging and extend life span

ai.headline: Bones release anti-aging proteins
ai.summary: Researchers studied the effect of exercise on bone cells in mice, finding that exercise triggers the release of anti-aging chemicals. The study focused on osteocytes, a type of bone cell. The findings suggest a potential link between bone health and aging.
ai.why_it_matters: Understanding how bones contribute to aging could lead to new strategies for promoting healthy aging and extending lifespan.
ai.life_skill: Try regular exercise to support bone health.
ai.fact: Exercise can trigger the release of anti-aging proteins from bone cells in mice.

quiz.question: What type of cells release anti-aging chemicals in response to exercise?
quiz.answer: Osteocytes release anti-aging chemicals in response to exercise.

items.title: Q&A: Hey AI, who should I vote for this year?

ai.headline: MIT researchers are tracking how AI chatbots answer questions about the 2026 U.S. midterm elections.
ai.summary: MIT professors Adam Berinsky and Chara Podimata have launched a project to monitor AI chatbot responses to election-related queries. The study aims to understand how these tools handle political questions during the 2026 U.S. midterm cycle.
ai.why_it_matters: As people increasingly use AI for information, understanding how these tools frame political topics is crucial for making informed decisions.
ai.life_skill: Check if an AI chatbot provides balanced sources when asking about political events.
ai.fact: AI chatbots are being systematically tracked for their responses to specific election questions.

quiz.question: What is the main goal of the MIT project described?
quiz.answer: To track how AI chatbots respond to questions about the 2026 U.S. midterm elections.

ai.caveat: This is a news report about a new project, not a completed study with final results or conclusions.

items.title: Comparison and effects of coordination based circuit training and small side games on agility and dynamic balance in healthy students aged 15-18 years
items.venue: Pedagogy of Physical Culture and Sports

ai.headline: Structured circuit training improves dynamic balance more than small-sided games in teenagers.
ai.summary: This randomised trial compared coordination-based circuit training, small-sided games, and regular school activity in 84 students aged 15–18. Both training types improved agility and dynamic balance compared to the control group, but circuit training produced significantly better dynamic balance scores than small-sided games.
ai.why_it_matters: Understanding which type of exercise targets specific motor skills helps young people choose activities that support better movement control and injury prevention.
ai.life_skill: Notice that different physical activities target different skills; structured drills may help with balance while games help with agility.
ai.fact: In this study, coordination-based circuit training was more effective than small-sided games for improving dynamic balance in adolescents.

quiz.question: Which intervention was better for improving dynamic balance?
quiz.answer: Coordination-based circuit training produced significantly higher dynamic balance scores than small-sided games.

ai.caveat: The study involved non-athlete students in Indonesia, so results may not apply to elite athletes or other populations.

items.title: Remote supervised exercise- and physical activity-based rehabilitation for post-stroke depression, anxiety, and quality of life: a systematic review, evidence map, and exploratory quantitative synthesis.

ai.headline: Exercise helps post-stroke depression
ai.summary: Researchers studied remote exercise programs for post-stroke depression and anxiety. They found a possible benefit for depression, but the evidence is fragile. The programs often included psychological support, making it hard to isolate the effect of exercise alone.
ai.why_it_matters: This research matters because it could help people recover from strokes and improve their mental health
ai.life_skill: Try incorporating physical activity into your daily routine to improve your mental wellbeing
ai.fact: Remote exercise programs can include a combination of physical activity and psychological support

quiz.question: What type of programs were studied for post-stroke depression and anxiety?
quiz.answer: Remote exercise- and physical activity-based rehabilitation programs

items.title: PROBLEMATIC SMARTPHONE USE, PHYSICAL ACTIVITY, AND OBESITY RISK IN CHILDREN AND ADOLESCENTS: A NARRATIVE REVIEW

ai.headline: Problematic smartphone use is linked to lower physical activity and higher obesity risk in young people.
ai.summary: This narrative review examined 45 studies on how problematic smartphone use affects physical activity and weight in children and adolescents. It found associations between heavy phone use, reduced movement, and excess body weight, though the evidence is mixed and mostly observational.
ai.why_it_matters: Understanding this link helps young people recognise how screen habits might be quietly replacing active time, which is crucial for long-term health.
ai.life_skill: Notice if you are scrolling instead of moving, and try swapping one hour of screen time for physical activity.
ai.fact: Reducing smartphone use has been associated with increased physical activity in some studies, but this does not prove it prevents obesity.

quiz.question: Did the review prove that using a smartphone causes obesity?
quiz.answer: No, the review found associations but noted that the observational evidence limits causal interpretation.

ai.caveat: The evidence is heterogeneous and predominantly observational, so it cannot establish that smartphone use directly causes obesity.

items.title: Psilocybin, cognitive stability and drinking reduction in co-occurring alcohol use disorder and depression: a pilot secondary analysis of a randomized, placebo-controlled trial

ai.headline: Psilocybin slowed task switching one week after dosing, but did not consistently change other thinking skills or willingness to try hard.
ai.summary: This pilot study looked at people with both alcohol use disorder and depression who took psilocybin or placebo in a randomized trial. About a week later, psilocybin slowed responses in cued task switching, but effects on other thinking measures were inconsistent and none were statistically robust after correction. Drinking fell in both groups and was linked to greater cognitive stability, while depressive symptoms improved more after psilocybin but were not tied to thinking changes.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that early pilot results about psychedelics and thinking should be treated as tentative, not proof, because the study was small and exploratory.

quiz.question: What did the study find about psilocybin and willingness to exert mental effort?
quiz.answer: There was no detectable effect on demand avoidance, which indexed willingness to exert control.

ai.caveat: This is a small pilot secondary analysis of a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, so the findings are preliminary and not proof.

items.title: Characterizing Rejection Sensitivity in Autistic Adolescents and Implications for Depression and Anxiety Symptoms

ai.headline: Feeling anxious about rejection is linked to social anxiety in autistic teens, but not depression.
ai.summary: This preprint surveyed 106 autistic adolescents to look at how rejection sensitivity relates to mental health. It found that while almost all participants experienced some rejection sensitivity, only the anxious type was linked to social anxiety symptoms, not depression or general anxiety.
ai.why_it_matters: Understanding that specific feelings of rejection anxiety connect to social anxiety can help young people and support workers identify specific stressors rather than assuming all rejection feelings lead to the same mental health issues.
ai.life_skill: Notice if your fear of rejection feels more like nervousness about social situations or anger, as these may affect your mood differently.
ai.fact: Rejection sensitivity is common in autistic adolescents, with higher rates observed in females and those with stronger autistic traits.

quiz.question: Did the study find that rejection sensitivity predicted depression in autistic adolescents?
quiz.answer: No, the study found that neither anxious nor angry rejection sensitivity predicted depression.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, and the observational design cannot prove that rejection sensitivity causes social anxiety.

items.title: Toward an Empirical Comparison of Bourdieu and Latour: Relational Theories in the Sociology of Poverty

ai.headline: Resources can help people in poverty while still leaving them dependent and financially insecure.
ai.summary: The study reanalysed twenty respondent files from an archive of 216 registrations collected in three Dutch urban areas. It found that skills could persist while their financial returns changed, contracts and payments could coexist with an inability to start work, and similar purchases could create different obligations toward future income.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows why practical help can improve someone’s situation without removing their ongoing money worries.
ai.life_skill: Check what ongoing costs or obligations come with any resource or payment before you rely on it.
ai.fact: A resource can be usable and valuable while still leaving a person dependent and financially insecure.

quiz.question: What did the study find about similar purchases made by people experiencing poverty?
quiz.answer: Similar purchases could create different obligations towards future income.

ai.caveat: It is a preprint not yet peer reviewed and based on a small, purposively selected set of files from Dutch urban areas.

items.title: Construction of a hierarchical linear regression prediction model for classical Chinese poetry writing ability development

ai.headline: Lower cognitive load and higher germane load are linked to better classical poetry writing in schoolchildren.
ai.summary: A one-year study of 1,920 Chinese primary school students tracked how classical poetry learning relates to writing ability. It found that higher intrinsic and extraneous cognitive load were linked to lower writing ability, while higher germane load was linked to higher writing ability, with schema construction, imagery processing, and emotional resonance partly explaining these links.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how mental effort during poetry learning may be linked to writing development, which could help teachers design better lessons.
ai.life_skill: Notice when poetry or writing feels mentally overwhelming and break the task into smaller steps.
ai.fact: Writing ability followed a mildly decelerating upward curve over the school year.

quiz.question: Which type of cognitive load was positively associated with writing ability?
quiz.answer: Germane cognitive load was positively associated with writing ability.

ai.caveat: This is a single observational study, so the results show links rather than prove cause and effect.

items.title: STRIDE: Stress Reduction in Dementia Caregivers

ai.headline: A trial will test whether a mindfulness app can reduce stress in dementia caregivers.
ai.summary: This is a planned randomised controlled trial comparing a smartphone mindfulness app called Healthy Minds Program with a general wellness app. It will look at whether the apps are feasible to use and whether they can lower caregiver stress, depression, anxiety, and improve mindfulness.
ai.why_it_matters: It could show whether a simple app might help people caring for someone with dementia manage their own stress and wellbeing.
ai.life_skill: Try using a reputable mindfulness app if you feel stressed, but check with a qualified professional if you need support.
ai.fact: Caregivers of people with Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias often experience high levels of stress.

quiz.question: What is the main aim of the STRIDE trial?
quiz.answer: To test whether a mindfulness app is feasible and may reduce stress, depression, anxiety, and improve mindfulness in dementia caregivers.

ai.caveat: This is a feasibility and proof-of-concept study, so it cannot yet prove the app works.

items.title: Cheap Retrieval and Observation Credit Assignment from One Quantity: The Value of Information

ai.headline: A new AI method uses one value score to decide which memories to retrieve and which observations deserve credit.
ai.summary: The paper studies memory in reinforcement learning, where finding relevant stored information is costly and assigning credit for useful memories across long sequences is hard. It proposes estimating a single quantity called the value of information from past experience using a learned world model. A pilot system using this signal solved a memory task with reduced context.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how AI agents might use memory more efficiently under energy and time limits, which matters for understanding how autonomous systems learn from experience.

quiz.question: What single quantity does the paper propose governs both memory retrieval and credit assignment?
quiz.answer: The value of information.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint not yet peer reviewed, and the results come from a pilot system rather than established evidence.

items.title: A multispecies foundation model for genome function prediction, gene annotation and sequence design

ai.headline: A new AI model can read, annotate and design DNA across many animal and plant species.
ai.summary: Researchers developed NTv3, an AI model trained on over 128,000 genomes and functional data from 15 animal and plant species. It predicts gene function, annotates genes and designs regulatory DNA sequences, matching or exceeding existing models across mammals, birds, fish, plants, fungi and protists.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how AI can help scientists understand and engineer DNA across species, which could affect agriculture, biodiversity and biotechnology.
ai.fact: NTv3 was pre-trained on more than 128,000 genomes using sequences up to 1Mb long.

quiz.question: What can NTv3 do with DNA sequences across species?
quiz.answer: It can predict function, annotate genes and design regulatory DNA sequences.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, so its findings are not yet confirmed.

items.title: The influence of working memory capacity and material complexity on the testing effect

ai.headline: Practising recall helps children learn, especially when material is made easier step by step.
ai.summary: Four experiments with fourth-grade pupils compared retrieval practice with restudy using materials of low and high complexity. Retrieval practice helped pupils with low working memory on simple material, while pupils with high working memory benefited more on complex material; repeated retrieval and diminishing-cues practice helped low-working-memory pupils with complex material.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how matching revision methods to material difficulty can help learners who find complex topics harder to remember.
ai.life_skill: Try practising recall with hints that gradually disappear when learning something complex.
ai.fact: Retrieval practice can improve learning compared with restudying, depending on material complexity and working memory capacity.

quiz.question: Which retrieval method helped pupils with low working memory learn complex material better than restudy?
quiz.answer: Diminishing-cues retrieval practice outperformed both cue-free retrieval practice and restudy.

ai.caveat: The study involved fourth-grade pupils in four experiments, so the results may not apply to older learners or other settings.

items.title: Unlocking Any-Order Generation in Pretrained Autoregressive Image Models

ai.headline: Existing AI image generators can be adapted to edit and fill in pictures without retraining from scratch.
ai.summary: The study looked at pretrained image generators that normally create images in one fixed order. Researchers added new position markers and a short training schedule so the same models could generate image parts in any order, improving inpainting and outpainting while keeping the usual fast inference tools.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how existing AI tools can be made more flexible for editing images without expensive retraining from scratch.
ai.life_skill: Try using AI image tools that support inpainting or outpainting to edit or extend pictures rather than starting from scratch.
ai.fact: Pretrained autoregressive image models can be adapted to generate image tokens in any order with modest extra compute.

quiz.question: What did the researchers adapt pretrained image models to do?
quiz.answer: Generate image tokens in any order so they can inpaint, outpaint, and edit images.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, so the findings are not yet confirmed.

items.title: [Correspondence] What kind of leader does WHO need?

ai.headline: The WHO will elect a new Director-General in 2027 to lead global health efforts.
ai.summary: The paper discusses the upcoming election for the World Health Organization's next Director-General. It outlines major health challenges the new leader will face, including climate change, evolving pathogens, pandemic preparedness, and vaccine hesitancy.

ai.life_skill: Notice that while technology can offer small cognitive boosts, consistent practice and sleep remain the most reliable ways to support memory.
ai.fact: Tingling and itching on the scalp were more common during active stimulation than during sham sessions, but no serious adverse events were reported.

quiz.question: How long did the memory improvements from stimulation last in this study?
quiz.answer: Significant pooled effects were observed within 1 day after stimulation, while longer-term estimates were imprecise.

ai.caveat: The study is a preprint not yet peer-reviewed, and the authors note that heterogeneity and small-study effects limit conclusions about long-term safety and durability.

items.title: Negative affectivity moderates the association between job demands and hair cortisol in healthcare workers: a cross-sectional multi-method study

ai.headline: Stress from certain job demands may raise long-term stress hormone levels more in people high in negative affectivity.
ai.summary: Researchers studied 67 healthcare workers in Northern Italy, measuring job demands, negative affectivity, and hair cortisol as a marker of long-term stress. Job demands were not linked to cortisol overall, but among people high in negative affectivity, problem solving and time pressure were more strongly linked to higher hair cortisol.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that personality differences can shape how workplace stress affects the body over time.
ai.life_skill: Notice whether time pressure or problem solving at work affects your stress more than it does for others, and consider discussing workload with a supervisor or occupational health professional.
ai.fact: Hair cortisol concentration is used as a biomarker of long-term activation of the body’s stress response system.

quiz.question: What did the study find about job demands and hair cortisol in people high in negative affectivity?
quiz.answer: Among people high in negative affectivity, problem solving and time pressure were more strongly linked to higher hair cortisol.

ai.caveat: This was a small cross-sectional study of 67 workers, so it cannot show that job demands cause changes in cortisol.

items.title: AB-Attention: Accurate Block Attention for Accelerating Video Diffusion Transformers

ai.headline: A new method speeds up AI video generation by skipping most attention calculations while keeping quality high.
ai.summary: The study tested AB-Attention, a training-free technique that approximates full attention in video diffusion transformers by selectively computing only important blocks of data. On two video models, it skipped 89–92% of attention work, improved image quality by up to 4.4 dB over the strongest baseline, and achieved up to 2.23 times faster end-to-end speedup.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how AI video tools can become faster and more efficient without losing visual quality, which could make them cheaper and more accessible in everyday use.
ai.life_skill: Try using AI video tools that advertise efficient or accelerated generation to save time and computing power.
ai.fact: AB-Attention can skip 89–92% of attention calculations in video diffusion transformers while maintaining or improving quality.

quiz.question: What did AB-Attention achieve compared to baselines in terms of attention computation?
quiz.answer: It skipped 89–92% of attention, whereas baselines computed 1.8–3.6 times as much.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint not yet peer reviewed, and the findings are based on technical experiments with two specific video models rather than real-world user trials.

items.title: [Series] Charting a course to men's health and wellbeing: applying a lens of power and politics to improve men's health outcomes
authors: Sarah J Hawkes, Srinivasa Vittal Katikireddi, Kent Buse, Sally Theobald, James W F Catto, James A Smith, Sabina Faiz Rashid, Rachel Tolhurst, John L Oliffe, Peter Baker, Beatrice R Egid, Laura Dean, Webster Mavhu, Beate Ringwald, Rachel M Thomson, Ishrat Jahan, Chukwuebuka Ugwu, Derek M Griffith

ai.headline: Men's health gets little policy attention despite poor outcomes, especially among marginalised men.
ai.summary: The paper examines why men's health has received limited and uneven attention in health policy and practice. It highlights that gendered and intersectional aspects of men's health have been especially overlooked, particularly among socially or structurally marginalised men.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how policy gaps can leave specific groups of men with worse health and shorter lives.
ai.life_skill: Notice how social factors like income or background can shape health outcomes for different groups.
ai.fact: Men, particularly those who are socially or structurally marginalised, experience poor health and life expectancy outcomes.

quiz.question: Which group of men is highlighted as especially overlooked in health policy?
quiz.answer: Men who are socially or structurally marginalised.

ai.caveat: This is a commentary paper proposing strategies rather than presenting new experimental evidence.

items.title: Living alone riskier for young and middle-aged adults than seniors, study indicates

ai.headline: Living alone may raise death risk more for adults aged 18–64 than for seniors.
ai.summary: The study looked at living alone and death from many causes. It found that living alone appears to increase the risk of death, especially among adults aged 18 to 64.
ai.why_it_matters: It suggests living alone may be a health concern for younger and middle-aged adults, not just older people.
ai.life_skill: Notice how much social contact you have if you live alone and consider staying in regular touch with others.
ai.fact: Living alone appears to be linked to a higher risk of death from multiple causes, particularly in adults aged 18 to 64.

quiz.question: Which age group appeared to have a higher risk of death linked to living alone?
quiz.answer: Adults aged 18 to 64 appeared to fare worse than seniors.

ai.caveat: This is a news report of a study, not the full research, so the design and strength of the evidence are unclear.

items.title: A decade of carbon dioxide data from space gets an upgrade

ai.headline: NASA satellites are getting an upgrade to measure carbon dioxide from space more accurately.
ai.summary: Two NASA instruments, OCO-2 and OCO-3, take over a million daily observations of sunlight reflecting off Earth. An algorithm uses the physics of light travelling through air to turn these readings into atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations.
ai.why_it_matters: Better satellite data helps scientists track where carbon dioxide is coming from and how it moves around the planet.
ai.life_skill: Check reliable sources such as NASA or your national weather service for information on atmospheric carbon dioxide levels.
ai.fact: OCO-2 and OCO-3 capture more than a million observations of sunlight reflecting off Earth's surface every day.

quiz.question: What do OCO-2 and OCO-3 measure from space?
quiz.answer: They capture sunlight reflecting off Earth's surface, which an algorithm converts into atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations.

ai.caveat: This is a news report describing a data upgrade, not a peer-reviewed study with testable results.

items.title: A single brain signal may explain schizophrenia's most puzzling symptoms

ai.headline: A weakened brain signal may link several puzzling symptoms of schizophrenia.
ai.summary: Researchers studied brain signals in people with schizophrenia and found that a weakened signal may connect sensory processing difficulties, disorganized speech, and greater symptom severity. The discovery could help explain how the disorder works and might lead to earlier detection and new treatments.
ai.why_it_matters: It offers a possible explanation for why seemingly unrelated symptoms of schizophrenia occur together.
ai.fact: A weakened brain signal may be linked to sensory processing difficulties, disorganized speech, and greater symptom severity in schizophrenia.

quiz.question: What did researchers find may connect several symptoms of schizophrenia?
quiz.answer: A weakened brain signal may connect sensory processing difficulties, disorganized speech, and greater symptom severity.

ai.caveat: This is a news report about a discovery, not the original research, so the findings have not been independently verified here.

items.title: Distinct gradients of cortical architecture capture visual representations and behavior across the lifespan

ai.headline: Two brain architecture gradients map how visual areas are organised and change across life.
ai.summary: Researchers used MRI to study the human visual cortex and found two gradients of cortical structure—one where cell and myelin features converge and another where they diverge. These gradients predict visual brain organisation and new visual representations, and each follows a different pattern across the lifespan.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that measurable brain structure can act as a fingerprint for how visual areas work and develop over time.
ai.fact: The visual cortex contains two distinct architectural gradients that relate to visual behaviour and change differently across the lifespan.

quiz.question: What did the two cortical gradients predict in the visual cortex?
quiz.answer: They predicted the structural and functional topography of the visual cortex, including the presence of new visual representations.

ai.caveat: This is a single observational study using MRI, so it shows links rather than proving cause and effect.

items.title: Representation, Innovation, and Product Adoption -- by Jennifer L. Kao, Tamar Oostrom

ai.headline: Paying for elderly people to join drug trials led to more trials and more drug use by older adults.
ai.summary: Researchers studied a 2000 Medicare change that lowered the cost of including elderly people in clinical trials. After the policy, sponsors included more older participants and ran more trials for diseases common in later life, especially for drugs not yet approved or being tested for new conditions. Elderly people also used more of the newly tested drugs.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how changing who is included in research can change which medicines get developed and who ends up using them.
ai.life_skill: Notice whether health research includes people like you, and ask whether results apply to your age group.
ai.fact: A policy change that lowered the cost of including elderly participants in clinical trials increased their representation and shifted drug development toward diseases common in older age.

quiz.question: What happened after Medicare expanded coverage of clinical trial costs for elderly participants?
quiz.answer: Trial sponsors included more elderly participants and ran more trials for diseases common among older people, leading to greater drug use by that group.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, and the findings come from observing a policy change rather than a randomised experiment.

items.title: Global nature talks reach deal but money remains an issue

ai.headline: Countries reached a global deal to halt nature decline, but funding remains unresolved.
ai.summary: Countries have been trying to get a global agreement to halt nature decline back on track. A deal has been reached at global nature talks. Money remains an issue.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how international agreements try to protect the natural world, while highlighting that paying for conservation is still a major sticking point.
ai.life_skill: Notice how nature in your local area is protected or funded, and consider supporting local conservation efforts.
ai.fact: Global nature talks can produce agreements to halt nature decline even when funding questions remain unresolved.

quiz.question: What remains an issue after the global nature deal was reached?
quiz.answer: Money remains an issue.

ai.caveat: This is a short news report, not a peer-reviewed study, so it provides limited detail and no evidence beyond the reported deal.

items.title: The Relationship Between Depression and Cognitive Function with the Level of Independence in Daily Living Activities Among Older Adults at Sabai Nan Aluih Sicincin

ai.headline: Depression and poorer thinking skills are linked to less independence in daily activities among nursing-home residents.
ai.summary: The study looked at 80 older adults in one nursing home and measured depression, cognitive function, and independence in daily living activities. It found that both depression and cognitive function were significantly associated with independence levels.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how mental health and thinking skills can affect everyday independence for older adults in care.
ai.life_skill: Notice whether low mood or memory difficulties are making daily tasks harder, and consider mentioning it to a care worker or health professional.
ai.fact: Depression and cognitive function are significantly associated with the level of independence in daily living activities among older adults.

quiz.question: What did the study find about depression and cognitive function in relation to independence?
quiz.answer: Both were significantly associated with the level of independence in daily living activities.

ai.caveat: This is a single cross-sectional study at one nursing home, so it shows a link but cannot prove cause and effect.

items.title: Sensory-based non-pharmacological interventions for reducing dental anxiety and improving behavioural cooperation in paediatric patients: a systematic review with GRADE assessment.

ai.headline: Sensory changes like adapted dental rooms, screens or music may lower children's dental anxiety and improve cooperation, but evidence is only moderate at best.
ai.summary: A systematic review of 47 studies, including 25 randomised or controlled trials, looked at sensory-based approaches such as sensory-adapted dental environments, audiovisual distraction or virtual reality, music therapy, aromatherapy and weighted blankets for children up to 18 years old. The strongest evidence supported sensory-adapted dental environments and audiovisual distraction or virtual reality, while music therapy had lower certainty; overall certainty ranged from very low to moderate because of bias, varied methods and imprecise results.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that simple, non-drug changes to the dental setting may help anxious children, though more high-quality research is needed before they become routine.
ai.life_skill: If a child feels anxious about dental visits, ask the dental team whether a calmer environment, headphones, music or a video could be used during treatment.
ai.fact: Dental anxiety affects an estimated 9%-20% of children and disproportionately impacts those with neurodevelopmental conditions.

quiz.question: Which sensory-based approaches had the strongest evidence for reducing children's dental anxiety and improving cooperation?
quiz.answer: Sensory-adapted dental environments and audiovisual distraction or virtual reality had moderate-certainty evidence, the strongest among the approaches reviewed.

ai.caveat: This is a systematic review of trials with overall low-to-moderate certainty, limited by risk of bias, heterogeneity and imprecise results, so it supports cautious use rather than proof of routine benefit.

items.title: Neonatal Sleep Disruption and Brain Development in Preterm Infants: A Narrative Review of Neurodevelopmental Outcomes

ai.headline: Sleep disruption in preterm babies may be linked to later brain and behaviour outcomes, but proof is limited.
ai.summary: The review looked at studies of preterm infants in neonatal intensive care and how noise, light, caregiving and painful procedures can disrupt sleep. It found that sleep disruption is linked to altered brain development, attention problems, attachment difficulties and stress system changes, though causes are hard to separate from prematurity and illness.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that protecting sleep in neonatal units could be a practical way to support long-term development in preterm babies.
ai.life_skill: Notice how noise, light and frequent handling might affect a baby’s sleep and consider quieter, clustered care where possible.
ai.fact: Sleep supports brain maturation, synaptic plasticity and white matter development in newborns.

quiz.question: What does the review say about the link between neonatal sleep disruption and later outcomes?
quiz.answer: It is linked to altered brain development, attention problems, attachment difficulties and stress system changes, but causal relationships remain difficult to establish.

ai.caveat: This is a narrative review of observational studies and meta-analyses, not a randomised trial, so it cannot prove that sleep disruption causes later problems.

items.title: Maternity versus non-maternity healthcare settings for the diagnosis of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy.
items.venue: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews

ai.headline: A Cochrane review found only one small trial comparing maternity and non-maternity settings for gestational diabetes screening, so no firm conclusion can be drawn.
ai.summary: The review looked for studies comparing maternity healthcare settings with non-maternity settings for diagnosing gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy. It found just one randomised trial with 781 participants, and because the trial analysed results by the setting people actually used rather than their original randomisation, its findings are unreliable. No other studies were identified.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that there is currently no reliable evidence about whether the type of healthcare setting affects gestational diabetes screening and diagnosis.

quiz.question: How many studies did the Cochrane review find comparing maternity and non-maternity settings for gestational diabetes screening?
quiz.answer: It found only one randomised trial with 781 participants.

ai.caveat: The review is based on a single small trial whose analysis method weakened the protections of randomisation, so the evidence is very uncertain.

items.title: Effect of virtual reality-based exergaming on multidimensional outcomes in individuals with cognitive impairment: a three-level meta-analysis based on the ICF framework

ai.headline: Virtual reality exercise games may improve thinking, movement and quality of life in people with cognitive impairment.
ai.summary: This review combined 22 randomised trials of virtual reality-based exergaming in people with cognitive impairment. It found possible improvements in memory, attention, executive function, balance, muscle strength, mobility and quality of life, but not in depressive symptoms, overall fitness or fall risk.
ai.why_it_matters: It suggests a non-drug activity that could support everyday independence for people with cognitive impairment.
ai.life_skill: Try short virtual reality exercise sessions if you or someone you support has cognitive impairment, after checking with a qualified health professional.
ai.fact: Virtual reality-based exergaming is linked to better balance and muscle strength in people with cognitive impairment.

quiz.question: Which outcome did the review find was not significantly improved by virtual reality exergaming?
quiz.answer: Depressive symptoms, comprehensive physical fitness and fall risk showed no significant effect.

ai.caveat: The included trials varied in quality and the evidence certainty was rated with GRADE, so the size of the benefit is not certain.

items.title: Problematic internet use among young people in Türkiye: a meta-analysis

ai.headline: Among young people in Türkiye, more time online is strongly linked to higher problematic internet use.
ai.summary: This meta-analysis combined 27 studies of 16,488 high school and university students in Türkiye. It found male students reported slightly higher problematic internet use than female students, those using the internet the most each day reported much higher problematic use than those using it the least, and family income showed no clear link.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that how long someone spends online is more closely tied to problematic internet use than gender or family income.
ai.life_skill: Notice how many hours you spend online each day and consider whether that time is crowding out sleep, study, or face-to-face contact.
ai.fact: The gender gap in problematic internet use among young people in Türkiye was small and appeared to be getting smaller in more recent studies.

quiz.question: Which factor was most strongly linked to problematic internet use in this meta-analysis?
quiz.answer: Students in the longest daily internet-use category reported substantially higher problematic internet use than those in the shortest category.

ai.caveat: All included studies were cross-sectional, so they show associations rather than prove that time online causes problematic internet use.

items.title: Apple Vision Pro: The good, the bad, the ugly

ai.headline: A review of early research on Apple Vision Pro finds benefits, technical limits, and unresolved ethical concerns.
ai.summary: The study reviewed 104 papers about Apple Vision Pro from 2024 to 2026. It found most research focuses on validated uses in medicine, education, and software, while risks, ethics, and harms are studied much less.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that early excitement about a new headset may outpace independent research into its risks and effects on people around the user.
ai.life_skill: Try checking independent reviews and privacy information before buying or using a new headset.
ai.fact: Most of the reviewed Apple Vision Pro research focused on benefits rather than documented risks or misuse.

quiz.question: What did the review find about the balance of research on Apple Vision Pro?
quiz.answer: Most included papers validated benefits, while research on risks and harms was comparatively thin.

ai.caveat: It is a preprint, not yet peer reviewed, and the included studies themselves vary in quality and design.

items.title: Causal Intervention Modeling of Exercise--Sleep--Mental Health for College Students from Multimodal Wearable Data

ai.headline: Researchers built a model to test whether changing exercise could improve sleep and mental health in college students.
ai.summary: The study used wearable data from two student datasets to model how reallocating time to exercise might affect next-night sleep and later mental-health outcomes. It describes a statistical approach called CISM that estimates these effects while accounting for observational treatment assignment and sparse mental-health assessments.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how wearable data could be used to understand whether lifestyle changes might influence wellbeing, rather than just spotting links.
ai.life_skill: Notice how changes in your daily activity relate to your sleep and mood over the following days.
ai.fact: The paper presents a modelling framework for estimating how exercise reallocation may affect sleep and mental health using observational wearable data.

quiz.question: What kind of data did the researchers use to study exercise, sleep and mental health?
quiz.answer: They used multimodal wearable data from two college student datasets.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not been peer reviewed and relies on observational data, so it cannot prove that exercise causes changes in sleep or mental health.

items.title: AI Incidents and Marginalized Populations: A Descriptive Analysis of the AI Incident Database (1983–2026) from a Social Work Perspective

ai.headline: Most documented AI harms are unintentional and happen after systems are already in use.
ai.summary: The study looked at 1,549 publicly reported AI incidents from 1983 to 2026. Most incidents occurred from 2020 onward, and among a subset of 214 coded incidents, discrimination and toxicity were usually unintentional and happened after the AI was already deployed.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that AI-related harm can affect everyday services like healthcare, education and law enforcement, often without anyone intending it.
ai.life_skill: Notice when AI tools are used in public services and ask how decisions are made and who is affected.
ai.fact: Among 214 coded AI incidents, 32.7% involved protected characteristics, most often race or ethnicity.

quiz.question: When did most discrimination and toxicity AI incidents happen relative to deployment?
quiz.answer: 97.6% occurred after the AI system was already in active use rather than during development or testing.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint not yet peer reviewed and describes publicly reported incidents, which may not capture all AI harms.

items.title: Cognition in healthy aging, ages 36 to 108: Associations with dementia risk factors and neurodegenerative disease biomarkers

ai.headline: Some lifestyle factors link to thinking test scores in later life, while brain changes link to faster decline.
ai.summary: Researchers studied 1,396 healthy adults aged 36 to 108 over about five years. Education, diabetes, motor function, hearing and vision were linked to how well people performed on thinking tests, but not to how quickly scores fell. Blood markers of Alzheimer’s disease were linked to lower scores from age 65 onward and to faster decline.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that everyday health factors may shape thinking ability in later life, while separate biological changes may drive decline.
ai.life_skill: Check your hearing and vision regularly and discuss any concerns with a health professional.
ai.fact: In generally healthy adults, thinking test performance and the rate of decline appear to be partly separate components.

quiz.question: Which factors were linked to thinking test performance but not to the rate of decline?
quiz.answer: Education, diabetes, low motor function, hearing loss and low vision were linked to performance, but none was linked to rate of decline.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, and as an observational study it cannot prove that the risk factors cause the differences in thinking performance.

items.title: Standing up heals: A qualitative analysis of participants' daily reflections from Emotion-Focused Training for Helping Professions (EFT-HP)

ai.headline: A 14-day emotion-focused training helped helping professionals shift from self-criticism and threat toward self-compassion and soothing.
ai.summary: Researchers analysed daily written reflections from 146 healthcare, social work, psychology and education professionals who completed a 14-day online Emotion-Focused Training for Helping Professions. Reflections moved from threat and self-criticism toward soothing and self-compassion, with self-criticism falling from 14.3% to 3.9% of units and the threat system dropping from 35.4% to 7.0%.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how structured emotional training may help people in caring roles manage burnout-related feelings in everyday life.
ai.life_skill: Notice when you are being self-critical and try to respond to yourself with the same kindness you would offer a friend.
ai.fact: Self-compassion was the most frequently coded category in participants’ reflections throughout the 14-day intervention.

quiz.question: What happened to self-criticism in participants’ reflections from Day 1 to Day 14?
quiz.answer: It fell from 14.3% to 3.9% of reflection units.

ai.caveat: This was a single-group qualitative study with no control group, so the changes cannot be assumed to be caused by the training.

items.title: Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging

ai.headline: High artificial sweetener use is linked to faster memory and thinking decline in adults.
ai.summary: Researchers studied nearly 13,000 adults and found that those consuming the most artificial sweeteners had a 62% faster decline in memory and thinking skills, equivalent to about 1.6 extra years of brain aging. Six popular sweeteners were linked to faster cognitive decline, but causation was not established.
ai.why_it_matters: It suggests a possible link between common sugar substitutes and brain health that people may want to consider when choosing drinks and foods.
ai.life_skill: Notice how often you use artificial sweeteners and consider cutting back if you use them daily.
ai.fact: People consuming the most artificial sweeteners experienced a 62% faster decline in memory and thinking skills.

quiz.question: What did the study find about people who consumed the most artificial sweeteners?
quiz.answer: They experienced a 62% faster decline in memory and thinking skills, equivalent to about 1.6 extra years of brain aging.

ai.caveat: This was an observational study, so it shows a link but cannot prove that artificial sweeteners cause faster brain aging.

items.title: Investor's Last Exam: Can AI Agents Do Equity Investment Without Seeing the Future?

ai.headline: AI agents can research stocks well but still struggle to forecast prices accurately.
ai.summary: Researchers created a benchmark called Investor's Last Exam to test AI agents on full equity research using only information available at the time. Top models scored around 68 out of 100 overall but only about 52 on forecasting and modelling, showing research skill does not easily translate into accurate predictions.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that even advanced AI cannot reliably predict future investment outcomes from available evidence, so human judgment remains important in financial decisions.
ai.life_skill: Check whether an investment claim is based on solid evidence or just a forecast before trusting it.
ai.fact: The benchmark uses a versioned financial database with validated timestamps to ensure AI agents cannot see future information when making judgments.

quiz.question: What did the top AI models score on forecasting and modelling in the benchmark?
quiz.answer: The leading model scored only 52.5 out of 100 on Forecast & Model.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, and the results come from a simulated benchmark rather than real-world investing.

items.title: A Case Formulation Approach to Cognitive Processing Therapy

ai.headline: A trial will test whether personalising trauma therapy improves veterans’ daily life and wellbeing.
ai.summary: Researchers are comparing standard Cognitive Processing Therapy with a personalised version that adds case formulation to target functioning, quality of life and wellbeing in US veterans with PTSD. Results are not yet reported, so it is not known whether the adapted therapy works better.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how mental health care may move beyond symptom reduction to help people rebuild everyday life after trauma.

quiz.question: What is the trial comparing?
quiz.answer: It compares standard Cognitive Processing Therapy with a personalised version that adds case formulation.

ai.caveat: This is a trial registration with results posted, not a peer-reviewed published study, so the findings are not yet confirmed.

items.title: [Editorial] Improving men's health in a changing world

ai.headline: Men globally face shorter lives and greater illness than women, driven by disease, injury, and substance use.
ai.summary: This editorial examines men's health worldwide. It finds that men have shorter life expectancies than women, a gap that has widened since the 19th century, and a 16% higher global burden of illness measured in disability-adjusted life-years. The main drivers include non-communicable diseases, external causes such as suicide and injuries, communicable diseases, and substance use.
ai.why_it_matters: It highlights a persistent global health gap that affects how long and how well men live compared with women.
ai.life_skill: Notice how social expectations around masculinity might discourage seeking help for physical or mental health issues.
ai.fact: Global disability-adjusted life-years are 16% greater among men than women.

quiz.question: What is one primary driver of the higher burden of illness among men mentioned in the editorial?
quiz.answer: Non-communicable diseases such as cardiovascular disease, cancer, and diabetes are primary drivers.

ai.caveat: This is an editorial, not original research, so it presents expert perspective rather than new evidence from a study.

items.title: PHACTn enables training-free, context-independent inference of nucleotide variant tolerance across the genome

ai.headline: A new computer tool predicts whether DNA changes are likely to be tolerated without needing training or powerful hardware.
ai.summary: Researchers developed PHACTn, a method that uses evolutionary relationships among mammals to judge whether single-letter DNA changes are likely to be tolerated. It performed better than existing tools on non-coding variants linked to disease in ClinVar and OMIM, using only four interpretable parameters and no GPU.
ai.why_it_matters: It could make it easier and cheaper to understand which genetic changes might contribute to disease, especially in poorly understood non-coding DNA.
ai.life_skill: Check whether a health-related claim about a DNA variant is based on peer-reviewed evidence before acting on it.
ai.fact: PHACTn is a preprint and has not yet been peer reviewed, so its findings are not yet confirmed.

quiz.question: What does PHACTn use to infer whether a DNA variant is tolerated?
quiz.answer: It traverses the mammalian phylogenetic tree and models evolutionary independence and distance from the query species.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint, not yet peer reviewed, so the results are preliminary and not yet confirmed.

items.title: Asking teachers to set high expectations leads to more detailed feedback and reveals subtle bias, study finds

ai.headline: Asking teachers to set high expectations leads them to give more detailed feedback.
ai.summary: The study looked at what happens when teachers are prompted to communicate high expectations and confidence in students' potential. It found that this prompting leads teachers to give more detailed feedback.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how a simple prompt can change the way teachers support students, which matters for everyday learning and fairness in education.
ai.life_skill: Notice whether your teachers give detailed feedback and ask them what they believe you can achieve.
ai.fact: Prompting teachers to communicate high expectations and confidence in students' potential leads them to give more detailed feedback.

quiz.question: What did prompting teachers to set high expectations lead to?
quiz.answer: It led them to give more detailed feedback.

ai.caveat: This is a news report about a study, not the full research paper, so the design, sample size and peer-review status are not described.

items.title: MCT1-dependent mitochondrial lactate import sustains cardiac metabolism

ai.headline: Mouse hearts can keep working by turning lactate into energy when the usual fuel pathway is blocked.
ai.summary: Researchers studied mouse heart tissue to see how it gets energy when the main way of importing sugar breakdown products into mitochondria is missing. They found that a different transporter, MCT1, allows lactate to enter the mitochondria, where it is converted into energy, helping the heart function normally and resist stress.
ai.why_it_matters: This reveals a backup system for how our heart generates energy, which could help explain how the body adapts to stress or disease.
ai.fact: In mouse hearts, lactate can be imported into mitochondria via MCT1 to sustain energy production even if the pyruvate carrier is absent.

quiz.question: What molecule does MCT1 import into the mitochondria in this study?
quiz.answer: MCT1 imports lactate into the mitochondria.

ai.caveat: The study was conducted on mice, so it is not yet proven that human hearts use this exact backup mechanism in the same way.

items.title: The optimum medical policy is a moving goalpost

ai.headline: Medical best practice often shifts as evidence improves, like oxygen targets for premature babies.
ai.summary: The piece describes how oxygen treatment for premature babies was linked to blindness, then restricted, which lowered blindness but increased deaths. Over decades, clinical trials helped the specialty converge on a narrower oxygen target that balances both risks. The author uses this as an example of medical advice swinging like a pendulum before settling.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that today’s ‘optimum’ medical advice may change as measurement and evidence improve, so health guidance should be treated as current rather than permanent.

items.title: scTGCL: A Transformer-Based Graph Contrastive Learning Approach for Efficiently Clustering Single-Cell RNA-seq Data

ai.summary: The study tested scTGCL, a Transformer-based graph contrastive learning tool, on twenty real and simulated single-cell RNA sequencing datasets. ai.why_it_matters: It helps scientists understand cell types and biological processes more reliably, which can improve research into health and disease.
